title: KnowProxy: Adapting Large Language Models by Knowledge-guided Proxy
claim: A small proxy trained on knowledge elicited from a frozen large model adapts to the task without needing output probabilities, and routes at inference.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: concept sketch, training flow, inference flow with side inset
description: Three labeled panels, (a) Concept, (b) Training and (c) Inference. Panel (a) is a geometric sketch of nested ellipses for the task distribution. Arrows start at 'LLM' and point to two dots. The 'Zero-shot' arrow reaches a point outside the target region. The 'Knowledge' arrow plus the brown 'Fine-tuning Proxy' arrow reach a point inside the darker region. A grayscale bar runs from simple to complex. Panel (b) is a vertical stack of boxes. A question and a {x,y} database feed a frozen Private/Large LM (lock icon), which produces knowledge k. That knowledge goes into a {x,y,k} database, then into the Open/Small LM, which outputs y^SLM. Panel (c) shows the same two LMs and a 'Confident?' routing decision that sends the query either to the small LM's output or to the LLM's. A dotted inset at the right shows an example with textual knowledge, confidence scores, and a final combined confidence. Blue boxes mark the large LM and beige boxes mark the small LM.
caption: Conceptual illustration of KNOWPROXY. (a) A smaller proxy model is trained using textual knowledge generated by LLMs to capture the target task distribution better. (b) During training, knowledge is elicited from LLMs via prompting and incorporated as an auxiliary input to the proxy. (c) At inference, KNOWPROXY utilizes multiple confidence scores from LLMs to perform dynamic routing, thereby balancing efficiency and accuracy.
abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) using smaller proxy models has been shown to improve training efficiency, where the LLMs remain frozen while the proxies are tuned on top. However, this approach typically requires access to the output probability distributions of LLMs, which are often inaccessible or unstable. To address this limitation, we propose KnowProxy, a knowledge-guided proxy framework in which the proxy is trained with textual knowledge rather than probability distributions. Specifically, we first elicit textual knowledge and reasoning from frozen LLMs through prompting, and then the proxy model learns to adapt this reasoning to target task distributions. We evaluate KnowProxy on diverse reasoning benchmarks with different fine-tuning scenarios. Comprehensive results show that KnowProxy achieves competitive or even better performance without direct access to probability distributions, thereby providing a scalable and versatile alternative to traditional fine-tuning.
